source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΙΘʹ. Εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους τεσσαράκοντα μάρτυρας. Μαρτύρων μνήμης τίς ἂν γένοιτο κόρος τῷ φιλομάρτυρι; διότι ἡ πρὸς τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς τῶν ὁμοδούλων τιμὴ ἀπόδειξιν ἔχει τῆς πρὸς τὸν κοινὸν Δεσπό την εὐνοίας. Δῆλον γὰρ, ὅτι ὁ τοὺς γενναίους ἄνδρας ἀποδεχόμενος ἐν τοῖς ὁμοίοις καιροῖς οὐκ ἀπολειφθήσεται τῆς μιμήσεως. Μακάρισον γνησίως τὸν μαρτυρήσαντα, ἵνα γένῃ μάρτυς τῇ προαιρέσει, καὶ ἐκβῇς χωρὶς διωγμοῦ, χωρὶς πυρὸς, χωρὶς μα στίγων, τῶν αὐτῶν ἐκείνοις μισθῶν ἠξιωμένος. Ἡμῖν δὲ οὐχ ἕνα πρόκειται θαυμάζειν, οὐδὲ δύο μόνους, οὐδὲ μέχρι δεκάδος ὁ ἀριθμὸς πρόεισι τῶν μακαρι ζομένων· ἀλλὰ τεσσαράκοντα ἄνδρες, ὡς μίαν ψυχὴν ἐν διῃρημένοις σώμασιν ἔχοντες, ἐν μιᾷ συμπνοίᾳ καὶ ὁμονοίᾳ τῆς πίστεως, μίαν καὶ τὴν πρὸς τὰ δεινὰ καρτερίαν, καὶ τὴν ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας ἔν στασιν ἐπεδείξαντο. Πάντες παραπλήσιοι ἀλλή λοις, ἴσοι τὴν γνώμην, ἴσοι τὴν ἄθλησιν. Διὸ καὶ ὁμοτίμων τῶν στεφάνων τῆς δόξης κατηξιώθησαν. Τίς ἂν οὖν ἐφίκοιτο λόγος τῆς τούτων ἀξίας; Οὐδὲ τεσσαράκοντα γλῶσσαι ἐξήρκεσαν ἂν τοσούτων ἀνδρῶν ἀρετὴν ἀνυμνῆσαι. Καίτοι, εἰ καὶ εἷς ἦν ὁ θαυμαζόμενος, τήν γε τῶν ἡμετέρων λόγων δύναμιν ἐξήρκει καταπαλαῖσαι, μὴ ὅτι πλῆθος τοσοῦτον, φάλαγξ στρατιωτικὴ, σύστημα δυσκαταγώνιστον, ὁμοίως ἔν τε πολέμοις ἀήττητον καὶ ἐν ἐπαίνοις ἀπρόσιτον. Δεῦρο δὴ οὖν, εἰς μέσον αὐτοὺς ἀγαγόντες διὰ τῆς ὑπομνήσεως, κοινὴν τὴν ἀπ' αὐτῶν ὠφέλειαν τοῖς παροῦσι καταστησώμεθα, προδείξαντες πᾶσιν, ὥσπερ ἐν γραφῇ, τὰς τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀριστείας. Ἐπεὶ καὶ πολέμων ἀνδραγαθήματα καὶ λογογράφοι πολλάκις, καὶ ζωγράφοι διασημαίνουσιν, οἱ μὲν τῷ λόγῳ διακοσμοῦντες, οἱ δὲ τοῖς πίναξιν ἐγχαράττοντες, καὶ πολλοὺς ἐπήγειραν πρὸς ἀνδρίαν ἑκάτε ροι. Ἃ γὰρ ὁ λόγος τῆς ἱστορίας διὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς παρ ίστησι, ταῦτα γραφικὴ σιωπῶσα διὰ μιμήσεως δεί κνυσιν. Οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀναμνήσωμεν τῆς ἀρετῆς τῶν ἀνδρῶν τοὺς παρόντας, καὶ οἱονεὶ ὑπ' ὄψιν αὐτῶν ἀγαγόντες τὰς πράξεις, κινήσωμεν πρὸς τὴν μίμησιν τοὺς γενναιοτέρους καὶ οἰκειοτέρους αὐτοῖς τὴν προαίρεσιν. Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι μαρτύρων ἐγκώμιον, ἡ πρὸς ἀρετὴν παράκλησις τῶν συνειλεγμένων. Οὐδὲ γὰρ καταδέχονται νόμοις ἐγκωμίων δουλεύειν οἱ περὶ τῶν ἁγίων λόγοι. Διότι οἱ εὐφημοῦντες ἐκ τῶν τοῦ κόσμου ἀφορμῶν τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν εὐφημιῶν λαμβάνουσιν· οἷς δὲ ὁ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται, πῶς δύναταί τι τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ ἀφορμὴν παρ έχειν εἰς περιφάνειαν; Οὐκ ἦν μία πατρὶς τοῖς ἁγίοις· ἄλλος γὰρ ἀλλαχόθεν ὥρμητο. Τί οὖν; ἀπόλιδας αὐτοὺς εἴπωμεν, ἢ τῆς οἰκουμένης πολίτας, Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς τῶν ἐράνων συνεισφοραῖς τὰ παρ' ἑκάστου καταβληθέντα κοινὰ τῶν εἰσενεγκάντων γίνεται· οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν μακαρίων τούτων ἡ ἑκάστου πατρὶς κοινὴ πάντων ἐστί· καὶ πάντες εἰσὶ πανταχόθεν ἀντιδιδόντες ἀλλήλοις τὰς ἐνεγκού σας. Μᾶλλον δὲ τί δεῖ τὰς χαμαὶ κειμένας περιζη τεῖν, ἐξὸν τὴν νῦν αὐτῶν πόλιν, ἥτις ἐστὶν, ἐννοεῖν Πόλις τοίνυν μαρτύρων ἡ πόλις ἐστὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ· ᾗ. τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεὸς, ἡ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἡ ἐλευθέρα, ἡ μήτηρ Παύλου, καὶ τῶν ἐκείνῳ παραπλησίων. Γένος δὲ τὸ μὲν ἀνθρώπινον ἄλλο ἄλλου· τὸ δὲ πνευματικὸν ἓν ἁπάντων.
thought_title: The Forty as one soul and a common city
orientation: Basil opens his homily by asking why the memory of martyrs can never satisfy a lover of martyrs, and he introduces the Forty as one soul in many bodies whose praise is beyond human speech.
pass_a_gloss: Homily 19. On the holy forty martyrs. Of the memory of martyrs what satiety could there be for the lover of martyrs? Because the honor toward the good fellow-servants has a demonstration of the goodwill toward the common Master. For it is clear, that the one who accepts the noble men will not be left behind in imitation in similar times. Bless genuinely the one who bore witness, in order that you may become a martyr by choice, and may come out without persecution, without fire, without scourges, having been deemed worthy of the same rewards as those. But for us not one is set before us to marvel at, nor only two, nor does the number of those being blessed go forward up to a ten; but forty men, as having one soul in divided bodies, in one shared breath and concord of faith, displayed one endurance also toward terrible things, and one resistance on behalf of the truth. All similar to one another, equal in mind, equal in contest. Therefore also they were deemed worthy of crowns of glory of equal honor. What word then could reach the worth of these? Not even forty tongues would have sufficed to hymn the virtue of so many men. And yet, even if the one being marveled at were one, he would have sufficed to throw down the power of our words, not to mention so great a multitude, a military phalanx, a system hard to overcome, alike unconquered in wars and unapproachable in praises. Come then, bringing them into the midst through remembrance, let us establish the common benefit from them for those present, having shown beforehand to all, as in a painting, the brave deeds of the men. Since also the feats of wars both speech-writers often and painters indicate, the ones adorning with speech, the others engraving on tablets, and both stirred many toward courage. For what the speech of history presents through hearing, these things painting silently shows through imitation. So then let us also remind those present of the virtue of the men, and as if bringing their deeds under their eyes, let us move toward imitation the more noble and more akin to them in choice. For this is the praise of martyrs, the exhortation toward virtue of those gathered together. For the speeches about the saints do not accept to be enslaved to the laws of encomia. Because those who speak praise take the beginnings of their praises from the starting points of the world; but for those to whom the world has been crucified, how can anything in it provide a starting point for distinction? There was not one fatherland for the saints; for one had set out from one place, another from another. What then? Shall we call them cityless, or citizens of the inhabited world? For as in the contributions of shared meals the things deposited by each become common to those who contributed; so also in the case of these blessed ones the fatherland of each is common to all; and all are from everywhere giving back to one another the lands that bore them. But rather why is it necessary to seek out the things lying on the ground, when it is possible to consider their present city, which it is? The city of martyrs then is the city of God; of which the craftsman and maker is God, the Jerusalem above, the free one, the mother of Paul, and of those similar to him. And the race, the human one, is one from one, another from another; but the spiritual one is one of all.

pass_b_english: What satiety could there ever be in remembering the martyrs for someone who loves martyrs? For the honor we give to good fellow-servants proves our goodwill toward the common Master. It is clear that the one who welcomes brave men will not be left behind in imitating them when similar times come. Bless the martyr sincerely, and you become a martyr by choice: you depart this life without persecution, without fire, without scourges, and are counted worthy of the same rewards as they are.

For us, though, it is not one man set before us to admire, nor only two, nor does the number of the blessed reach only as far as ten. Forty men, holding one soul in divided bodies, displayed one shared breath and one concord of faith, one endurance in the face of dangers, and one resistance on behalf of the truth. All were alike to one another, equal in resolve, equal in contest. Therefore they were counted worthy of crowns of equal honor and glory.

What speech, then, could reach the worth of these men? Not even forty tongues would have been enough to hymn the virtue of so many men. And yet, even if only one were being admired, he would have been enough to overpower the strength of our words—let alone such a multitude, a military phalanx, a company hard to overcome, alike unconquered in wars and unapproachable in praises.

Come then, let us bring them into our midst through remembrance and make their benefit common to all who are present, displaying the men's brave deeds to everyone as if in a painting. For historians often mark out brave deeds in wars, and painters do as well—the one adorning them with words, the others engraving them on tablets—and both have stirred many toward courage. What the word of history presents through hearing, painting shows in silence through imitation.

So let us also remind those present of the virtue of these men, and, as it were, bring their actions before their eyes, and move the more noble and those close to them in resolve toward imitation. For this is the praise of martyrs: the call to virtue for those who have gathered. Words about the saints do not consent to be enslaved to the rules of encomium. For those who speak praises take the starting points of their praises from the world's resources; but for those to whom the world has been crucified, how can anything in it provide a starting point for renown?

The saints did not have one fatherland; each had set out from a different place. What then? Should we call them cityless, or citizens of the whole world? For just as in contributions to a common feast what each one puts in becomes common to all who contributed, so also for these blessed ones each one's fatherland is common to all, and all of them give their native lands to one another in exchange from every direction.

But why should we search out the lands that lie on the ground, when it is possible to consider their present city, which is what it is? The city of the martyrs, then, is the city of God. Its craftsman and builder is God: the Jerusalem above, the free one, the mother of Paul and of those like him. Their human lineage, one different from another; but their spiritual lineage is one for all.
